results.experiment: Exp 34b — sub-square criterion RETEST with real pruning (Pythia-410M)

preregistered.S1: ascending (lowest lmin@T/2) worse than random (inversion extends)

honest_verdict: The sub-square measurement carries WEAK but REAL signal — in the OPPOSITE direction from the square-point measurement. At sub-square, pruning the lowest-lmin heads (those collapsed even at T/2) yields BETTER perplexity than random (65k vs 114k). This makes geometric sense: heads collapsed even at T/2 are the extreme cases — their key geometry is so degenerate that they carry little retrieval signal. BUT the practical value is minimal: all three strategies produce catastrophic perplexity (65k-114k vs baseline 45) at 20% pruning on this model. The 1.75x separation (ascending vs random) is much weaker than the 67x separation at square point in GPT-2. The two measurements (square and sub-square) probe DIFFERENT properties: square-lmin measures within-head retrieval sharpness (low = vital); sub-square-lmin measures across-head degeneracy ranking (low = extreme = prunable).
implications: 1) The sub-square recipe from Exp 34 is CONFIRMED as a signal (the correlation was real) but its direction is OPPOSITE to what we pre-registered: at sub-square, the lowest-lmin heads are the prunable ones. 2) The two measurements cannot be used interchangeably: square-lmin says 'keep the low ones', sub-square-lmin says 'prune the low ones' — they measure different things. 3) At 20% pruning on a 24-layer model, ALL strategies are destructive: the useful pruning range is much smaller. 4) Follow-up needed: 5% and 10% pruning rates to find the non-destructive range.
